findings.title: There's a new way to break RSA that's faster than anything we've seen before
findings.summary_md: Dan Goodin's article is the first mainstream coverage, published roughly a day before the cyberpress.org story in this event list. It quotes co-author Nadia Heninger of UC San Diego and Allurity's Karsten Nohl, and frames the cost: forging a 1024-bit RSA signature took about 2^65 operations and 1,380 core-years, versus an estimated 2^80 operations and 500,000 to 1 million core-years to factor the same key. It also identifies Privacy Pass, used by Apple and Cloudflare, as the best-known blind-RSA deployment, where an attacker would need roughly 2^43 token requests.

findings.title: Forging 1024-bit RSA signatures in nearly SNFS time
findings.summary_md: The original researcher disclosure, received by the IACR ePrint archive on 2026-09-20 and approved 2026-09-22, by Laura Shea, Miro Haller, Adam Suhl, Nadia Heninger and Emmanuel Thome. The authors implemented the 2007 Joux-Naccache-Thome algorithm, spending 1,380 CPU core-years over five calendar months and 2^32 oracle queries so any signature on a 1024-bit key can later be forged offline in about 180 core-years. They conclude RSA with a signing oracle loses 15 to 30 bits of concrete security across the 1024-bit to 4096-bit parameters, leaving even 4096-bit RSA below a 128-bit level in that model.

findings.title: When e-th Roots Become Easier Than Factoring
findings.summary_md: The two-decade-old algorithm the new attack implements, received by the ePrint archive on 2007-11-18, by Antoine Joux, David Naccache and Emmanuel Thome. As characterized by the 2026 paper, it lets an attacker with temporary access to a raw RSA signing or decryption oracle forge signatures in time close to the special number field sieve without factoring the modulus. The 2026 work is its first published end-to-end implementation at 1024-bit scale.
